Before you start The examples use HTTP, the rules software follows to send a request over the web and receive a reply. No account or API key is needed for this guide. No installation is needed to read this guide. Explore the case by track System designDefine the report contract Algorithms & dataCheck that you have every batch Software & productionHandle an interrupted report Measurement & MLInterpret credited conversions AI engineeringGive an agent a bounded reporting tool Run the samples locally Twelve conversions. Then fifteen. Then fourteen. At 9 a.m., an advertising report says yesterday's campaign generated 12 conversions. At 3 p.m., it says 15. The following morning, it says 14. Each number may be a valid observation made at a different time. Advertising reports combine records that can arrive late, out of order or more than once. Understanding the result requires knowing what the platform counted and what the client retrieved. We will follow a fictional retailer advertising a coffee grinder on 21 November 2026. The example uses UTC reporting dates and GBP. The task is to establish what the report tells us, what may still change, and which decisions the evidence supports. Explore System design Where the numbers come from A customer sees an advertisement, clicks it and purchases the grinder that afternoon. The advertising platform records an impression, a tracking service records a click, and the retailer records an order. A browser integration or server-side conversion API then notifies the advertising platform about the purchase. These systems may have different clocks, identifiers and delivery guarantees. The platform must validate the records, determine which belong together and decide whether the purchase qualifies for attribution. Some purchases may be unobservable or impossible to match. A conceptual model is: Event collection → Validation and identity resolution → Attribution → Aggregation → Reporting API These are processing responsibilities, not necessarily separate services. The model does not describe any advertising company's private infrastructure. From individual events to reporting rows An event describes an occurrence; a reporting row contains calculations over a group of events. Our retailer requests daily campaign performance and receives: Metric Reported value Impressions 8,000 Clicks 320 Spend £160 Attributed conversions 12 All figures, identifiers and campaign events in this article are hypothetical. The account is retailer-uk, the campaign is coffee-grinder, and the reporting date is 21 November 2026. From an event to a reporting row Scroll across to follow the diagram. A text explanation is available below. INDIVIDUAL EVENTS · COFFEE-GRINDER CAMPAIGN CONCEPTUAL PROCESSING STAGES Advertising deliveryImpression An ad is displayed; an impression record is created. Interaction recordClick A click identifier connects the interaction to the campaign. Retailer + integrationPurchase O-1042 An order produces a purchase notification. IngestionCollect and validate Receive records that may be late, repeated or invalid. Identity resolutionMatch and deduplicate Link eligible records. Recognise repeated purchase notifications. AttributionAssign conversion credit Apply the report's conversion definition and attribution rules. Aggregation → Reporting API · retailer-uk / coffee-grinder / 21 Nov 20268,000 impressions · 320 clicks · £160 spend · 12 attributed conversions One campaign/day observation. Individual event IDs and arrival order are absent from this aggregate row. A conceptual teaching model, not a provider architecture. The event examples contribute to a larger fictional campaign; they are not the only events counted in the row. Read “From an event to a reporting row” as text An impression, click and purchase are separate records. Purchase O-1042 is one business occurrence even if its notification arrives more than once. Conceptual ingestion validates records; identity resolution matches and deduplicates them; attribution determines conversion credit. These responsibilities need not be separate services. Aggregation changes the grain from individual events to account/campaign/reporting-day totals. This observation is retailer-uk / coffee-grinder / 21 November 2026: 8,000 impressions, 320 clicks, £160 spend and 12 attributed conversions. This row omits individual event identifiers and processing order. Adding country as a dimension changes the aggregation key. A later snapshot can replace this observation without creating additional campaign activity. For this report, the aggregation key consists of account, campaign and reporting date. Adding country as a dimension adds country to the key. Two rows for the same campaign and date but different countries are legitimate groups, not duplicates. Keep three concepts distinct: The aggregation key identifies a group within a report. The report definition specifies scope, dimensions, metrics and calculation rules, including attribution settings. The snapshot identity distinguishes observations collected at different times. Matching row keys do not make reports comparable if their definitions differ. Ignoring either distinction can overwrite legitimate rows or combine incompatible observations. Even a date is a calculation rule A purchase at 00:30 UTC on 22 November belongs to that date in a UTC account, but may belong to 21 November in an account reporting farther west. Some systems assign conversions to the advertising interaction's date rather than the purchase date. The API contract must establish which rule applies. Currency also constrains aggregation: combining spend across currencies requires an explicit conversion policy and exchange-rate basis. Correct arithmetic cannot compensate for an incorrectly defined measurement. Why yesterday's report changes Assume three additional eligible purchase notifications are processed between our first and second observations. The purchases happened during the relevant period, but the information needed to credit them arrived later. Event time is when the purchase happened. Processing time is when a system handles its notification. Consider three purchases: Scroll across to compare all columns → Purchase Event time Processing time A 21 Nov, 18:10 21 Nov, 18:11 B 21 Nov, 20:15 22 Nov, 11:40 C 21 Nov, 19:05 22 Nov, 13:20 C happened before B but was processed after it. Network delays, scheduled uploads and integration failures can all make processing order differ from event order. The problem with closing a reporting window At midnight, a system counting purchases by event date can publish immediately or wait for more notifications. Waiting may improve coverage, but delays useful information and does not, without an external guarantee, prove that every event has arrived. Stream-processing systems manage this trade-off explicitly. In Apache Beam, a window groups events into a time interval, a watermark estimates progress through event time, and a trigger determines when an aggregation result is emitted. Depending on configuration, later information can update a provisional result. Source: Apache Beam: Windowing, watermarks and triggers. Watch the aggregate change Our simplified processor counts 12 eligible purchases at 09:00, then processes three more for the same reporting date: 12 + 3 = 15 The new aggregate supersedes the earlier observation. This illustrates the temporal problem; it does not establish that an advertising platform uses Beam or this update mechanism. Freshness is not finality Metrics can mature at different rates. Impressions and clicks may become reportable relatively quickly, spend may need reconciliation, and conversions depend on event delivery, matching and attribution. OpenAI's Ads reporting documentation describes distinct update schedules for these metrics. Source: OpenAI: Ads reporting documentation. A report collected five minutes ago can still contain provisional conversion data. An attribution window defines which outcomes qualify for credit after an interaction; it does not necessarily guarantee that all eligible records have arrived or become immutable. Claim finality only when the platform documents that guarantee. Later information has raised our count to 15. The next morning, it falls to 14. When one purchase becomes two events The retailer sends browser-side and server-side notifications for the same order. Treating them as independent purchases can count one business event twice. Correct counting therefore depends on identity. Messages are not purchases Retries create a similar problem. If a sender receives no acknowledgement, it cannot tell whether the notification was lost or processed. Retrying improves delivery but may produce a second copy. A stable business-event identifier can help recognise repeated submissions: purchase_id = O-1042 Two notifications with that identity may describe one purchase. A second purchase, O-1043, must remain distinct even if the customer, amount and approximate time match. Deduplicating by those attributes alone could erase legitimate activity. Meta's recommended browser/server deduplication method matches both event identifier and event name. Those rules belong to Meta's contract; they are not universal matching rules for advertising platforms. Source: Meta: Handling Duplicate Pixel and Conversions API Events. Why exactly-once processing is not enough A framework may replay an event after failure while committing its effect on managed state exactly once. Flink documents this guarantee through checkpoint recovery; end-to-end guarantees also depend on the sources and output systems. Source: Apache Flink: Fault tolerance. But two different event identifiers can describe the same purchase. Applying each exactly once still counts two conversions. Processing guarantees cannot repair an incorrect business identity. Three reconciliation problems therefore need different identities. Event deduplication recognises records for the same occurrence. Reporting-row reconciliation recognises the same aggregate group within one report definition. Snapshot reconciliation determines when a newer observation replaces an earlier one. Why our report falls from 15 to 14 Assume a duplicate purchase notification was initially counted and later removed: 15 − 1 = 14 This correction is hypothetical, not a claim about any provider's production deduplication schedule. A client collecting both snapshots must not add them. If they describe the same aggregate under the same definition, 14 is the newer observation. Preserve 15 for audit history if useful, but distinguish it from an additional fact to sum. Reconciliation requires the report definition, full aggregation key and observation identity; the latest value still need not be final. When the API returns only part of the answer Our analyst requests campaign performance. The client receives a first page and continuation token, then loses the connection while requesting page two. Its accepted rows can be valid while the requested report remains incomplete. This failure is independent of late source events. Pagination does not automatically provide a snapshot Pagination divides a result into retrievable pieces. A client follows continuation tokens until the API says no pages remain. Whether those pages form a consistent snapshot depends on the documented contract. Google Ads Search, for example, documents cached query results and page tokens; SearchStream returns results through a streaming response. Consistency within a cached retrieval does not make the metrics immutable across later queries. Sources: Google Ads API: Page through results, Search and SearchStream. Retries must preserve the original question A timeout alone may not reveal whether a request reached the server or its response was lost. A read-only retry may be appropriate under the API's limits and token rules, but it must preserve the original account, dates, dimensions and attribution configuration. Use bounded retries, backoff and explicit failure states. If a required page cannot be retrieved, retain accepted rows and mark collection incomplete. Pagination and partitioning solve different problems Pagination divides one query result; partitioning divides a task into smaller queries. A monthly report might use one query per day, each with its own pages. The collector must finish those pages and verify that its partitions cover the intended scope without unintended overlap. Every submitted query can succeed while a day that was never requested remains missing. Successful API calls alone cannot prove scope coverage. Explore Algorithms & data Recovery requires more than saving a cursor After a crash, a useful checkpoint identifies the original query, completed partitions, accepted pages and continuation state. Tokens remain usable only under the API's rules. If one expires or cannot be resumed safely, restart the affected partition and reconcile its replacement observations without double-counting. Two clocks, two kinds of completeness Scroll across to follow the diagram. A text explanation is available below. EVENT TIME PROCESSING TIME CLIENT RETRIEVAL · A SEPARATE OPERATION 21 Nov · 18:0022 Nov · 00:0009:0015:00 UTCACBACB Page 1Accepted rows Valid observations are retained. Page 2Request times out A required page is still missing. Collection stateRetrieval incomplete This can happen even when source data is mature. A, B and C use the purchase times in the article's table. The API-page failure is a separate hypothetical collection; time on the source timeline does not measure pagination progress. Read “Two clocks, two kinds of completeness” as text Both timelines use the same UTC scale. Purchase A happens on 21 November at 18:10 and is processed at 18:11. C happens at 19:05; B happens later, at 20:15. B is processed on 22 November at 11:40, before C at 13:20. Event order A, C, B becomes processing order A, B, C. The sloping lines show delay, not another purchase. Late eligible notifications can revise an earlier conversion count. Retrieving every page cannot force those source events to arrive or establish finality. Separately, a collector accepts page 1 but times out on page 2. That is incomplete retrieval, regardless of the source's maturity. Either problem can exist without the other. Four properties, not one status Validate a report against four questions: Property Question Retrieval completeness Did the client retrieve every required page and partition? Scope coverage Does the result cover the requested accounts, dates, dimensions and metrics? Data maturity Have the underlying metrics reached a suitable processing state for this use? Decision suitability Does the evidence support the intended interpretation or action? These properties are related, but none guarantees the others. If nine of ten pages contain £900 in compatible, non-overlapping spend rows, £900 is their subtotal, not a verified total for the request. Receiving the final page resolves that retrieval gap without establishing conversion finality or causal impact. Explore Software & production What the reported conversions actually mean The collector now holds the complete available report: 14 attributed conversions. Whether advertising caused 14 additional purchases is a different question. Attribution assigns credit Attribution rules determine which observed conversions receive credit for ad interactions. They may specify eligible clicks or impressions, windows, matching information, reporting dates and attribution models. A customer already planning to buy the grinder might see an ad, click and purchase. The purchase can qualify for attribution even if it would have happened anyway. The report cannot directly observe that alternative outcome. Incrementality requires a counterfactual The causal question is: how many purchases happened because of the advertising that would not otherwise have happened? A controlled experiment helps estimate the outcome without the campaign. Suppose eligible customers are randomly assigned to treatment and control groups. Treatment customers are eligible for the advertising intervention; control customers are withheld from it under the experiment's design. We compare their outcomes: Scroll across to compare all columns → Group Customers Purchases Treatment 10,000 120 Control 10,000 100 The purchase rates are 1.2% and 1.0%, a difference of 0.2 percentage points. Under appropriate randomisation and measurement assumptions, this difference helps estimate the intervention's incremental effect. It does not mean advertising caused all 120 treatment purchases or that the observed difference is the exact effect. Sampling uncertainty, interference and implementation failures matter. Google's Conversion Lift documentation provides a production example of treatment/control comparisons for advertising impact. Source: Google Ads: Conversion Lift. A complete report can still support the wrong conclusion Suppose attributed conversions rise by 20% after a budget increase. Seasonal demand, a price reduction, inventory or competing campaigns could explain the change. The report has not isolated the budget increase's causal effect. Attributed reporting can support monitoring and operational decisions under explicit assumptions. Claims about additional sales require evidence that addresses the causal question. An agent recommending budget changes must preserve that distinction. Explore Measurement & ML Building a report another system can safely use The retailer asks an agent: "Should we increase the coffee-grinder campaign budget tomorrow?" A successful reporting call does not establish that the evidence supports a recommendation. The reporting service needs to expose what it retrieved and the conditions under which the figures can be used. Make the guarantees explicit A proposed consumer-side evidence envelope can include: Scope: account, period, time zone, currency, dimensions and metric definitions. Collection: completed pages and partitions, failures and verified coverage. Maturity: collection time, source freshness and known revision limitations. Provenance: source API, query identity and observation identifier. Semantics: attribution settings, reporting grain and missing-value definitions. Limitations: uncertainty and unsupported conclusions. This is an application design, not an existing OpenAI Ads response schema. Its purpose is to make the report's properties machine-checkable. The same report can be acceptable for one use and rejected for another A report with all requested pages and correct scope can still contain provisional conversions. A dashboard may display it with a freshness warning, while a budget-change workflow requires more mature metrics, a longer comparison period and additional performance evidence. Suitability depends on the intended use. The boundary between evidence and action Scroll across to follow the diagram. A text explanation is available below. READ-ONLY REPORT · EVIDENCE VALIDATION ACTION WORKFLOW · SEPARATE AUTHORITY Report envelopeLatest observation: 14 Carry scope, coverage, maturity, provenance and limitations. Application checksValidate evidence Does this report cover the intended comparison and required metrics? Decision policyCheck suitability Enforce maturity rules, decision assumptions and proposal permission. If either check failsReturn the limitation or request more evidence Keep accepted observations. The agent cannot override a failed application check. RecommendationPropose a budget change State the exact campaign, change and supporting assumptions. ApprovalAuthorise that change An authorised person or policy approves the specific action. ExecutionSubmit the permitted change Use a separately authorised write operation. VerificationCheck platform state Confirm the budget reached its intended value; sales impact still needs evidence. A proposed application boundary. Passing the evidence checks permits a recommendation under policy; it does not itself grant approval, API write access or proof of incremental sales. Read “The boundary between evidence and action” as text The report envelope carries the latest observation of 14 attributed conversions together with scope, collection evidence, maturity, provenance, semantics and limitations. Application logic validates evidence and applies the workflow's decision policy before an agent can submit a recommendation. A missing requirement returns a limitation or a request for more evidence. If checks pass, the agent may recommend a specific budget change. An authorised person or policy must approve that action before a separately authorised write operation executes it. Verification checks that the intended platform state was reached. A confirmed budget change does not prove that sales improved or that any improvement was caused by advertising. An enforceable decision boundary Before an agent submits a budget-change proposal, a policy might require: Scope matching the campaign and comparison period. Every required page and partition collected. Available metrics meeting the workflow's maturity policy. A specified decision model with explicit assumptions. Permission to propose the specific action. Enforce these checks in application logic. A failed condition returns a limitation or requests more evidence. The agent cannot override the policy by producing a persuasive paragraph. Recommendation is not execution Keep four operations distinct: Recommendation: The agent proposes a specific budget change. Approval: An authorised person or policy approves it before execution, with human approval where required. Execution: A separately authorised operation submits the change. Verification: The system checks whether the intended platform state was reached. A proposal does not establish that the budget changed. A confirmed budget change does not establish that sales improved or that advertising caused the improvement. Explore AI engineering Test your understanding Apply the distinctions to three situations before opening the answers. Case A: The missing page Nine of ten pages contain £900 in spend. The final page repeatedly fails. Can the collector report £900 as total campaign spend? Read the answer Answer: No. It is the subtotal of compatible, non-overlapping received rows. A required page remains missing, so the complete requested total is unknown. Case B: The late conversion Every page arrives, but the platform documents that recent conversion metrics may change. Is the report complete? Read the answer Answer: Retrieval and scope may be complete while conversions remain provisional. Preserve both facts. Case C: The budget recommendation Attributed conversions rise by 20% after a budget increase. An agent recommends another increase because the first "caused more sales." What is missing? Read the answer Answer: Causal evidence. A recommendation may be defensible under an explicit operational policy, but attributed growth alone does not prove incremental sales. A causal claim needs stronger evidence, such as a well-designed experiment. What a trustworthy report actually guarantees Our 12 → 15 → 14 sequence exposes several independent guarantees: event identity determines what counts; processing determines when information arrives; report definitions determine what rows mean; and collection validation establishes what the client received. Measurement assumptions then constrain the conclusions. A useful report carries those boundaries forward. Keep accepted rows with missing coverage, provisional figures with their collection time and revision limits, and unavailable metrics as missing values. A null conversion count must not silently become zero, and an attributed count must not become a claim of incremental sales. This discipline applies to financial dashboards, marketplace analytics and operational monitoring as well as advertising. The result should make clear what is known, what may still change, and what the evidence permits us to do next. Can you use this report? Optional practice: compare five prepared outcomes from a separate fictional UK account. Open the examples to inspect complete, empty, partial, stale and rejected collections. Prepared examples · Fictional data The request in each example Get daily impressions, clicks, spend and credited conversions for campaigns in a fictional UK ad account on 1 and 2 November 2026. Time zone and currency London time, GBP Conversion credit 30 days after a click or one day after a view. Results use the date of the ad interaction. Open an example to see what came back and what you can do with it. Complete reportThe final batch arrived What came back Both batches arrived, giving you three rows. Each row covers one campaign and day. Impressions 2,300 Clicks 64 Spend £36.00 Credited conversions Total unavailable One row shows zero conversions and another has no conversion count. The spend total covers all the returned rows, but there isn’t enough information to add up conversions. What to do next Use the spend total for the requested period. Record when you collected it and check for later updates before using recent figures to make a decision. Empty reportThe request finished with zero rows What came back The first batch was empty and said there were no more batches. There are no totals to show. No rows matched the request. That gives you no spend or conversion figures to interpret. What to do next Check the account, dates and filters. If those are right, report “no rows returned” and keep the totals blank. Partial reportAnother batch is missing What came back The first batch returned two rows and a marker for the next batch. The next batch never arrived. Rows received 2 Spend in rows received £30.50 £30.50 is the subtotal for the rows you have. The spend for the full period is still unknown. What to do next Keep the original dates and filters and use the saved marker to retry the missing batch. If you can’t recover it, label the report partial and carry the gap into any summary. Stale reportAll batches arrived, but the figures are old What came back At a review on 5 November, the team still had a complete report collected on 3 November. They refreshed the same dates and received revised figures. Same reporting dates, two collection times Metric 3 Nov, 09:00 5 Nov, 09:00 Spend £36.00 £36.30 Credited conversions Unavailable 3 Receiving every batch tells you the collection finished. It doesn’t tell you whether the platform has since updated the figures. What to do next Refresh the same request before using the old copy. Use the newer figures for the same dates, and retain both collection times so readers can see what changed. Rejected requestThe requester lacked access What came back In this example, the reporting tool refused the request because the signed-in person didn’t have permission for the selected account. It returned no report. The tool stopped at its access check. There are no figures to interpret for that account. What to do next Check that you selected the right account and ask an account admin to confirm your access. Retry once the account or permission has been corrected. Try the collector and keep the evidence Optional implementation: the local reporting collector exercises pagination, bounded retries and partial results using separate fictional fixtures. Each invocation starts a fresh run. Durable checkpoints and live collection remain design work; samples need no advertiser account. For live requests, use the OpenAI Insights API reference. General Insights is paginated. Oversized dedicated conversion reports return HTTP 413 without rows or a cursor, requiring smaller entity lists or non-overlapping date ranges. OpenAI reporting limits Keep advertiser credentials on the server and enforce account access. The downloads below are illustrative application references. Use OpenAI’s documentation for the exact requests your software can send. The Harness downloads use made-up examples to explain how you might model ad selection or collect reports.
